questions.q: Which class provides a convenient API for timing how long operations take?
Which class helps implement toString() methods?
Which class helps implement equals() methods?
Which class is a fast and thread-safe alternative to SimpleDateFormat?
Which method checks whether a string is empty, null or only whitespace?
Which method shortens a string and ends it with an ellipsis?
Which method changes the first character of a string to title case?
Which validation method throws an exception when an argument is null?
Which class is a mutable wrapper around an int value?

We read the user's region from a legacy config value and pass it to commons-lang3 to build a java.util.Locale. Values like "_GB" work and give a country-only locale, but one customer has "_gb" stored and we get java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Invalid locale format: _gb. Java's own Locale constructor accepts lowercase country codes, so why does commons-lang reject this string, and where is that decision made?

Our CSV importer uses the commons-lang3 math helper that turns a string into the best-fitting Number subtype (Integer, Long, BigInteger, Float, Double, BigDecimal). Inputs like "42L" and "1.5d" work, but a row containing "1.5L" fails with java.lang.NumberFormatException: 1.5L is not a valid number. Why is a decimal value with an L type suffix rejected instead of just being truncated or parsed as a double, and which method makes that call?

We guard a server port setting with the commons-lang3 precondition helper that checks a long lies between a lower and upper bound. Configuring port 65535 with bounds 1 and 65535 is accepted, but a typo of 70000 makes startup fail with java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: The value 70000 is not in the specified inclusive range of 1 to 65535. We never supplied that message text ourselves. Which method builds this message, and are the bounds treated as inclusive or exclusive?

We use the commons-lang3 string helper that tests whether a string is made only of digits to check an amount field before calling Long.parseLong. It returns false for "-42", "+42", "12.5" and the empty string, yet it returns true for Devanagari digits such as "\u0967\u0968\u0969", which then makes our own parsing logic misbehave. Why does it accept non-ASCII digits but reject signs and decimal points, and where is that rule implemented?

Feature flags are read from a properties file and converted with the commons-lang3 boolean helper. "true", "TRUE", "yes", "on", "y" and even "1" all turn the feature on, but a flag written as "true " (trailing space left in the file) silently comes out as off, and "enabled" is also treated as off. No exception is thrown. Why does a trailing space make the value unrecognised, and which method decides which strings map to TRUE, FALSE or null?
